all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli provided by a computer, in which a person's actions partially determine what happens and which replaces the user's sense of reality without requiring the physical existence of objects or places.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: virtual environment
concepts.definition: Virtual environment is a non-real, computer-generated graphical representation of a real or imaginary world, populated with artificial objects, that is experienced through computer-generated sensory stimuli.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: marker
concepts.definition: A marker is a real-world object or image placed in the environment that a system detects to identify its position or track a user's motion and to place digital content at that position.

defining_facts.text: Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications use markers placed in the environment to trigger an augmented experience, and when a device detects a marker, the desired digital content appears at that marker's position in the real-world view.
Markers used in marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications include quick response (QR) codes, simple color codes, color bars, and fiducial markers.
Marker-based augmented reality (AR) applications are easier to build but difficult to maintain because markers are prone to damage, and a damaged marker may make the application not work.

Markerless augmented reality (AR) applications are more versatile than marker-based augmented reality applications, do not require physical markers, can use computer vision techniques, and allow users to decide where to place virtual objects.

concepts.name: field of view
concepts.definition: Field of view (FOV) is an angular measure of the region visible to the eye at a single point in time, and in virtual reality it is the amount of virtual environment visible.

defining_facts.text: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.
Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).

An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
Field of view (FOV) is the amount of virtual environment that is visible at any moment.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts.

A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience.
A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.
A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.
Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

concepts.name: locomotion
concepts.definition: Locomotion is the motor component of navigation in a virtual world, the actual movement between two locations, carried out by techniques that let a user move and perceive that the movement has taken place.

defining_facts.text: Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

Control over motion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement, is an aspect of locomotion that directly affects presence and indirectly affects cybersickness (CS) through presence; greater presence in virtual reality (VR) generally reduces cybersickness, and more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence.

The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.
The travel part of navigation, also called locomotion, is the motor component of navigation and refers to the actual movement between two locations.
Locomotion techniques, alternatively travel techniques, are techniques employed to let a user travel in a virtual world from one place to another and to perceive that travel has taken place.

Travel in navigation can be done by exploration, search, or maneuvering: exploration has no explicit goal or target point and the user moves around to see, learn, or explore; search is moving to a specified target location; and maneuvering comprises short, precise movements that change the viewpoint or break a path into small segments to reach a destination.

Travel in navigation can be accomplished using four broad types of locomotion techniques: walking-based locomotion, steering-based locomotion, selection-based locomotion, and manipulation-based locomotion.

concepts.name: teleportation
concepts.definition: Teleportation is a virtual reality locomotion operation in which a user selects a virtual target location and the virtual viewpoint instantly changes from the current location to that target, without physical movement.

defining_facts.text: The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

Teleportation in virtual reality (VR) is a locomotion operation in which a user can pull up a menu, point to a desired virtual location, and be sent to that location without making any physical movement.

Target selection-based locomotion techniques include teleportation, which instantly changes the virtual viewpoint from the current location to the target location, map dragging, in which the user fixes a location to move there instantly, and the jumper technique in cave-type systems.

Route planning-based locomotion is a selection-based locomotion technique in which the user selects a route to the target rather than only the endpoint; there may be multiple routes, and while moving through the selected route, different viewpoint changes make the user feel movement along a path, providing more granular control over travel and slightly more natural movement than target-based teleportation.

Teleportation-type movement in a virtual world can be the best choice for reducing overall exposure duration because it provides instantaneous movement between two points at maximum speed, but it is not a natural movement and may not always be a good approach when naturalness is required.

concepts.name: tangible user interface
concepts.definition: Tangible user interface is a real-world object whose virtual avatar appears in a virtual world and that, by aligning the real world and the virtual world, provides feedback to the user's somatosensory system in place of computer-controlled haptic devices.

defining_facts.text: Real-world objects whose virtual avatars appear in a virtual world and that are used in place of computer-controlled haptic devices to provide feedback to the user's somatosensory system are sometimes called tangible user interfaces.
The basic idea for implementing tangible user interfaces is to create the experience by aligning the real world and the virtual world.

concepts.name: location awareness
concepts.definition: Location awareness is a wayfinding feature for ascertaining a path through the environment to a desired destination and transferring spatial knowledge to the real world.

defining_facts.text: Location awareness in the Majuli virtual reality (VR) Tour case study was identified during contextual inquiry (CI) as an issue for users exploring a large space, and a possible resolution was to add a location awareness feature, later to be converted into functional requirements during system design.

concepts.name: navigation
concepts.definition: Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

In the design of immersive experiences, interaction is broadly categorized into three categories: object interaction, which is interacting with virtual objects in the immersive virtual world; navigation, which is moving from one point in the virtual world to another point with the corresponding change in viewpoint and mostly does not involve object interaction, although some navigation techniques may require it; and system control, which is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus, and is unlike object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation.
The goal of navigation in a virtual world is to move the user from one point to another, which means a change of the user's field of view or viewpoint.
The movement involved in navigation in a virtual world has two parts: the travel part and the wayfinding part.
Navigation has two components: locomotion or travel, which is the motor component, and wayfinding.

concepts.name: interaction for system control
concepts.definition: Interaction for system control is an interaction technique in immersive environments that issues commands to change system state, mode, or system-related settings.

defining_facts.text: Interaction in immersive environments is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and interaction for system control, where object interaction means selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment, navigation means moving from one point to another in the virtual environment, and interaction for system control means interaction required to change system-related settings.

Interaction for system control is an interaction technique whose goal is to issue commands that change system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file, and these commands are most of the regular operations associated with using any software.

Interactive methods for system control include physical controllers such as buttons and switches; graphical menus, adapted two-dimensional (2D) menus suitable for three-dimensional (3D) massive environments, one degree of freedom menus, and three-dimensional widgets; voice commands; gesture commands such as mimic gestures, symbolic gestures, sweeping gestures, sign language, speech-corrected hand gestures, and whole-body interactions; tools such as physical tools, virtual tools, and tangible interfaces; and multimodal interaction techniques that combine multiple techniques, for example voice with gestures or other interactions.

concepts.name: object manipulation
concepts.definition: Object manipulation is an interaction technique in immersive environments that, typically after selection, modifies a virtual object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior.

defining_facts.text: In any virtual experience, object interaction is broadly of two types: selection, which specifies one or more objects from a set of virtual objects in the virtual world, and manipulation, which interacts with a selected object to change its properties; the two types mostly have separate interaction techniques.
Object manipulation is the modification of an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, behavior, and others, and it typically follows selection of the object.
Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, that are related to virtual objects.

concepts.name: go-go technique
concepts.definition: The Go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant virtual objects that uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, allows the user to change virtual arm and hand length interactively, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so distant objects can be reached quickly.

defining_facts.text: Hand selection techniques for virtual objects include virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven selection.

The go-go technique is a virtual hand selection technique for distant objects that allows the user to interactively change the virtual arm length, the length of the virtual hand, uses one-to-one mapping when the target is close, and, as distance increases, maps smaller physical hand movements to larger and faster virtual hand movements, possibly exponentially, so that distant objects can be reached quickly.

The go-go technique has a low-precision problem for selecting distant small objects because the virtual hand moves faster when the object is farther away, so a small physical hand movement can miss, bypass, or cross the target and is difficult to control.

For selecting distant objects, prism may provide a better solution than go-go because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, and the ability to stop the virtual hand when the physical hand stops is not present in go-go.

In hand selection techniques, go-go and prism are travel techniques, intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique, and intent-driven selection may be combined with a go-go or prism travel technique.

concepts.name: three-dimensional widget
concepts.definition: A Three-dimensional widget is a simple indirect manipulation technique that places controls directly in a 3D scene with virtual objects, so manipulating a widget manipulates its associated object; each widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom.

defining_facts.text: Three-dimensional (3D) widgets are a simple indirect manipulation technique in which controls are placed directly in the 3D scene with virtual objects, and manipulating a widget manipulates the associated virtual object.

Each three-dimensional (3D) widget is typically responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom, so a single widget may not be sufficient to manipulate all properties of a given object; instead, specified sets of degrees of freedom are manipulated using the individual widgets.

concepts.name: world in miniature
concepts.definition: World in miniature (WIM) is an indirect proxy that provides a miniature handheld model of a virtual environment, representing all objects in the virtual world. Manipulating a model object manipulates the corresponding virtual object, even if it is outside the user's reach; moving certain model objects can also change the virtual viewpoint.

defining_facts.text: World in miniature (WIM) is a type of indirect proxy that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment, which represents all objects in the virtual world, so manipulating an object in the miniature model manipulates the corresponding actual object in the virtual world.

World in miniature (WIM) allows manipulation of virtual objects both within and outside the user's reach; for a distant object, the user does not need to select it, but can manipulate its representation in the miniature model, which then manipulates the distant object.
Implementing world in miniature (WIM) for large and complex virtual environments is not very practical because creating the miniature model for such environments is very difficult.
Manipulation-based locomotion can be implemented using a combination of the go-go technique, homer technique, and world in miniature metaphor.
In a world in miniature metaphor, moving or manipulating certain objects causes a corresponding change in the virtual viewpoint, as if the user moves from one place to another.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: Three-dimensional space is the space with x, y, and z axes in which an object can have three translational and three rotational degrees of freedom.

never_defined.name: interaction technique
never_defined.definition: An interaction technique is a method used in virtual reality to select or manipulate virtual objects, navigate a virtual world, or issue system-control commands.

never_defined.name: user experience
never_defined.definition: User experience is a key concern in virtual reality system design that is enhanced by reducing cybersickness, affected by presence, and supported by wayfinding and environment design.

never_defined.name: steering-based locomotion
never_defined.definition: Steering-based locomotion is a type of locomotion technique used to accomplish travel in navigation.

never_defined.name: surrounding physical environment
never_defined.definition: Surrounding physical environment is the real-world surroundings of a VR user that is part of the VR system because it can affect user behavior through real-world stimuli.

never_defined.name: button
never_defined.definition: A button is a physical controller and input device used for system control, including in non-tracked handheld controllers and navigation tools.

never_defined.name: voice command
never_defined.definition: Voice command is one of the interactive methods for system control.

never_defined.name: map
never_defined.definition: A map is a way of showing a real or virtual space or place, including objects or points, the user's current position, and routes, and can be updated to support wayfinding, movement, real-time tracking, or forming mental models.

never_defined.name: system state
never_defined.definition: System state is the state of a system that users perceive and that user interactions or commands can change to reach a goal state.

never_defined.name: direction
never_defined.definition: Direction is the orientation of a sound source, an object to be selected, or user movement in two- or three-dimensional space, used to describe sound-source location, support object selection, and support wayfinding.

never_defined.name: mental model
never_defined.definition: Mental model is a spatial knowledge base of the surroundings and overall environment that consists of landmark, procedural, and topological knowledge to make locating oneself and identifying a suitable path easier.

never_defined.name: virtual navigation
never_defined.definition: Virtual navigation is the movement in a virtual space produced by translating or mapping a user's physical movement.

never_defined.name: immersive hardware
never_defined.definition: Immersive hardware is hardware that is used with specialized devices to provide input in partial gait techniques.

never_defined.name: active walking interface
never_defined.definition: An Active walking interface is a specialized input device that may be used in partial gait techniques that map a user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in virtual space.

never_defined.name: pressure mat
never_defined.definition: A pressure mat is an active walking interface that can be used in partial gait techniques to provide input.

never_defined.name: pressure sensor
never_defined.definition: A pressure sensor is one of the active walking interfaces that may be used in partial gait techniques, in addition to other immersive hardware, to provide input and map a user's pattern of walking in a single place to different types of walking in the virtual space.

never_defined.name: linear treadmill
never_defined.definition: A linear treadmill is a specialized setup used in gait negation techniques.

never_defined.name: motorized floor tile
never_defined.definition: Motorized floor tile is one of the specialized setups used in gait negation techniques.

never_defined.name: human-sized hamster ball
never_defined.definition: A human-sized hamster ball is one of the specialized setups used in gait negation techniques.

never_defined.name: friction-free platform
never_defined.definition: A friction-free platform is a specialized setup used in gait negation techniques.

never_defined.name: bike locomotion platform
never_defined.definition: Bike locomotion platform is a physical setup or separate hardware used in physical steering-based navigation.

never_defined.name: virtual reality simulator
never_defined.definition: A virtual reality simulator is separate hardware involved in physical steering-based navigation, in which physically moving the steering controls results in travel in the virtual world.

never_defined.name: jumper technique
never_defined.definition: The jumper technique is a target selection-based locomotion technique in cave-type systems.

never_defined.name: cave-type systems
never_defined.definition: Cave-type systems are systems in which the jumper technique is used for target selection-based locomotion.

never_defined.name: homer technique
never_defined.definition: The homer technique is a technique that can be used, in combination with the go-go technique and the world in miniature metaphor, to implement manipulation-based locomotion.

never_defined.name: path
never_defined.definition: Path is a sequence of vertices or points of interest in a virtual world or graph that is followed to reach destinations and optimized for travel time and importance.

never_defined.name: destination
never_defined.definition: A destination is a desired location that a wayfinding path leads to or that a selected route in virtual vehicle travel moves the user to.

never_defined.name: landmark knowledge
never_defined.definition: Landmark knowledge is part of the spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model, covering the surroundings and other places.

never_defined.name: procedural knowledge
never_defined.definition: Procedural knowledge is knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path.

never_defined.name: topological knowledge
never_defined.definition: Topological knowledge is the spatial knowledge of the overall environment in a wayfinding mental model.

never_defined.name: knowledge base
never_defined.definition: A knowledge base is the essential collection of spatial knowledge in a wayfinding mental model, formed by landmark knowledge of surroundings and other places, procedural knowledge of the sequence of actions required to follow a path, and topological or map-like knowledge of the overall environment.

never_defined.name: locomotion or travel support
never_defined.definition: Locomotion or travel support is support in a virtual environment that, by itself, is not sufficient for wayfinding.

never_defined.name: compass
never_defined.definition: A compass is a direction indicator that can support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space.

never_defined.name: direction indicator
never_defined.definition: A Direction indicator is used to support wayfinding by specifying directions in two-dimensional or three-dimensional space.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: Two-dimensional space is a space in which a compass or direction indicator can specify directions to support wayfinding.

never_defined.name: command
never_defined.definition: A command is a regular operation in software use that changes system state or mode, such as launching an application, changing system settings, or opening a file.

never_defined.name: system mode
never_defined.definition: System mode is a mode of a system that can be changed by commands issued through interaction for system control.

never_defined.name: physical controller
never_defined.definition: A physical controller is one of the interactive methods for system control, for example a button or switch.

never_defined.name: switch
never_defined.definition: A switch is a physical controller used in interactive methods for system control.

never_defined.name: graphical menu
never_defined.definition: A graphical menu is an adapted two-dimensional menu suitable for three-dimensional massive environments, used as an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: two-dimensional menu
never_defined.definition: A two-dimensional menu is one of the interactive methods for system control, adapted to be suitable for three-dimensional massive environments.

never_defined.name: one degree of freedom menu
never_defined.definition: One degree of freedom menu is an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: gesture command
never_defined.definition: Gesture command is one of the interactive methods for system control, with examples including mimic gestures, symbolic gestures, sweeping gestures, sign language, speech-corrected hand gestures, and whole-body interactions.

never_defined.name: mimic gesture
never_defined.definition: A mimic gesture is a gesture command that is used as an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: symbolic gesture
never_defined.definition: A Symbolic gesture is a gesture command used as an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: sweeping gesture
never_defined.definition: Sweeping gesture is a gesture command used as an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: sign language
never_defined.definition: Sign language is one of the gesture commands used as an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: speech-corrected hand gesture
never_defined.definition: Speech-corrected hand gesture is a gesture command used as an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: whole-body interaction
never_defined.definition: Whole-body interaction is a gesture command, one of the interactive methods for system control.

never_defined.name: tool
never_defined.definition: A tool is one of the interactive methods for system control.

never_defined.name: physical tool
never_defined.definition: A physical tool is a tool that is an interactive method for system control.

never_defined.name: virtual tool
never_defined.definition: A virtual tool is a tool included among interactive methods for system control.
